record.paper_title: Ten Open Problems in Grammatical Inference
record.original_question: Under the negotiation-game winning criterion, can one find a winning deterministic learning algorithm when the two players' regular languages L1 and L2 are represented by deterministic finite automata with the same number of states, n1 = n2? A player wins if it identifies L1 ∩ L2 in the limit and either the opponent fails to identify that intersection or, when both identify it, the player makes fewer negative-query errors.

evidence.quote: Definition 12. Given a game ⟨L1, L2⟩and 2 players A and B, A wins if A identifies L1 ∩L2 in the limit and if either B identifies L1 ∩L2 in the limit and |errors(A)| < |errors(B)| or if B does not identify L1 ∩L2 in the limit.
Problem 10. Using definition 12, find a winning algorithm, in the case where n1 = n2.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Fix a finite alphabet Σ. For a regular language L ⊆ Σ*, let dfa-size(L) denote the number of states of the minimal deterministic finite automaton (DFA) accepting L.

A learner is a (deterministic) algorithm that, given an infinite presentation of examples for a target language T ⊆ Σ*, outputs a (possibly revised) hypothesis after each example and is said to identify T in the limit if its sequence of hypotheses stabilises on a representation of T.

Negotiation game. A game ⟨L1, L2⟩ involves two players A and B, where each player i ∈ {A, B} privately knows a regular language Li and is told the minimal DFA-sizes n1 = dfa-size(L1) and n2 = dfa-size(L2). The players exchange queries: each player may pose strings to the opponent who must classify them truthfully as members or non-members of the opponent's language. A "negative-query error" by a player is each instance in which that player issues a query whose answer (received from the opponent) is "no" (i.e., the queried string does not belong to the opponent's language). Let errors(P) denote the set (or count) of such negative-query errors made by player P throughout the play.

Winning criterion. Player A wins the play of ⟨L1, L2⟩ against player B if:
(i) A identifies L1 ∩ L2 in the limit, and
(ii) either B fails to identify L1 ∩ L2 in the limit, or B also identifies L1 ∩ L2 in the limit and |errors(A)| < |errors(B)|.

Problem. Restricting attention to instances in which n1 = n2 (i.e., the two players' minimal DFAs have the same number of states), exhibit a deterministic learning algorithm that, when used by a player, wins against every deterministic strategy of the opponent under the above winning criterion; or prove that no such algorithm exists.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface any publication that resolves the equal-size (n1 = n2) negotiation-game problem for learning the intersection of two regular languages under the stated winning criterion. The problem appears as one of a list of open problems in grammatical inference, and no follow-up work explicitly claiming a solution was located, so the current status is unknown.

status_evidence.snippet: Combines grammatical inference with game theory for control synthesis but does not address the equal-DFA-size negotiation winning algorithm.
status_evidence.claim: Related work does not appear to resolve the specific problem.
